CHAPTER 1 – INTRODUCTION TO PROCESS SYNCHRONIZATION

1.1 Introduction to Concurrency and Multithreading

In modern operating systems, concurrency refers to the ability of the system to manage multiple execution sequences simultaneously. Multithreading enables a single process to execute multiple sub-tasks in parallel across multiple CPU cores, sharing the same address space, memory heap, and system resources. While multithreading dramatically improves system throughput and responsiveness for I/O-bound and bursty workloads, it introduces fundamental coordination hazards when threads concurrently access mutable shared state.

1.2 Shared Data, Limited Resources, and Data Inconsistency

In resource reservation and ticketing platforms, the primary contended resource is a finite numerical integer: remaining seat capacity. When multiple concurrent buyer threads access this shared variable without synchronization barriers, non-deterministic execution interleavings corrupt the data state. Operations that appear atomic in high-level code (e.g., capacity = capacity - 1) actually decompose into three distinct hardware/OS instructions:

  1. Read (LOAD): Load the shared memory variable into a local CPU register.
  2. Modify (SUB): Decrement the register value by 1.
  3. Write (STORE): Store the modified register value back into shared memory.

If thread preemption or asynchronous I/O scheduling intervenes between the Read and Write phases, concurrent threads observe identical stale values, triggering severe data inconsistency.

1.3 Race Conditions and the Critical Section Problem

A race condition occurs when the outcome of concurrent execution depends unpredictably on the relative order or timing of thread execution. The portion of code that accesses, modifies, or writes to shared resources is formally designated as the Critical Section (CS). If two threads execute within their critical sections simultaneously, system invariants are breached. In ticket reservation systems, the most notorious manifestation is the Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race hazard, where multiple threads validate available quota ($1 > 0$) simultaneously, driving inventory below zero and producing duplicate seat assignments.

1.4 Overview of Synchronization Mechanisms (Mutex Locks & Semaphores)

To prevent concurrent threads from violating state invariants, operating systems provide synchronization primitives:

  • Mutex Lock (Mutual Exclusion): A binary locking mechanism designed for strict resource ownership. A thread must explicitly acquire() the lock before entering the critical section, and only the holding thread may release() it. At any moment, at most one thread executes inside the critical section.
  • Counting Semaphore: A generalized synchronization primitive initialized with an integer permit count $N$. Threads request permits via wait() (or acquire()) and surrender permits via signal() (or release()). Counting semaphores govern access to pools of identical finite resources.

1.5 Problem Statement and Product Requirements

The objective of this project—developed under Product 2: Mutex & Semaphore (Group 8) for Course 25CAI402PC203—is to engineer an end-to-end, high-throughput Event Registration Platform that guarantees Zero Overbooking under extreme concurrent loads.

  • Core Problem: During flash registration bursts (e.g., university hackathons, Tatkal quotas), hundreds of user requests contend for the final available seat ($C = 1$). Naive architectures oversell inventory, resulting in duplicate tickets, physical venue admission conflict, and financial chargebacks.
  • Product Requirements:
    1. Implement a deterministic multithreaded concurrency kernel in Python using threading.Lock (Mutex) and threading.Semaphore.
    2. Implement an unsynchronized baseline to actively reproduce and demonstrate the TOCTOU race condition ($C = -1$).
    3. Enforce Dijkstra’s 3 Critical Section criteria: Mutual Exclusion ($|C(t)| \le 1$), Progress, and Bounded Waiting ($O(k)$ FIFO queue).
    4. Build an executive web dashboard with real-time slot telemetry, payment authorization modals, procedural SVG QR boarding passes, and an automated refund reassurance flow.

CHAPTER 2 – OPERATING SYSTEM PRINCIPLES OF MUTEX & SEMAPHORE

2.1 Criteria for Critical-Section Solutions (Mutual Exclusion, Progress, Bounded Waiting)

Classical operating systems theory, formulated by Edsger W. Dijkstra (1965), dictates that any valid software or hardware solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three foundational criteria:

  1. Mutual Exclusion: If thread $T_i$ is executing in its critical section, no other threads may execute in their critical sections. Mathematically, for any time $t \ge 0$, the cardinality of active threads in the critical section $|C(t)| \le 1$.
  2. Progress Guarantee: If no thread is executing in the critical section and some threads wish to enter, only those threads not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding which will enter next. This selection cannot be postponed indefinitely, eliminating deadlocks.
  3. Bounded Waiting: A bound must exist on the number of times other threads are allowed to enter their critical sections after a thread has made a request to enter and before that request is granted. If $k$ requests arrive ahead of $T_i$, its waiting time is bounded: $Wait(T_i) \le k imes Δt_CS < \infty$, completely eliminating starvation.

2.2 Mutex Lock Operations: acquire(), Critical Section, and release()

A Mutex utilizes a binary state variable (_locked) and an associated wait collection:

  • acquire(): The thread queries the lock state. If _locked == False, it sets _locked = True atomically (Fast-Path) and proceeds into the critical section. If _locked == True, the calling thread is suspended and appended to an ordered FIFO wait queue (Slow-Path).
  • Critical Section: The isolated code region where capacity validation, seat reservation, and ticket ledger mutations are executed exclusively.
  • release(): The holding thread relinquishes the lock upon exiting the critical section. If waiting threads exist in the FIFO queue, the head of the queue is dequeued and granted ownership. If no threads are waiting, _locked reverts to False.
Mathematical Safety Invariant: For an event with initial capacity $C_total$, confirmed tickets $R(t)$, and remaining capacity $C_rem(t) = C_total - |R(t)|$, the system must unconditionally enforce:
∀ t ≥ 0,   0 ≤ Crem(t) ≤ Ctotal  ∧  |C(t)| ≤ 1

2.3 Counting Semaphores: Permit Management via wait() and signal()

A Counting Semaphore is initialized with an integer value $S$ representing the count of available identical resources (e.g., $S = N$ available event passes). The semaphore provides two standard atomic operations:

  • wait() (or acquire()): Decrements the semaphore value: $S \leftarrow S - 1$. If $S < 0$, the calling thread is blocked until another thread signals. In our implementation, non-blocking / timeout-bounded acquisitions are supported: if $S \le 0$, the request is immediately flagged as Sold Out.
  • signal() (or release()): Increments the semaphore value: $S \leftarrow S + 1$. If threads are suspended waiting for a permit, one thread is unblocked.

2.4 Comparison of Mutex Lock, Binary Semaphore, and Counting Semaphore

Property Mutex Lock Binary Semaphore Counting Semaphore
Permit Range Binary (0 or 1) Binary (0 or 1) Integer ($0 \le S \le N$)
Ownership Rule Strict: Only the lock acquirer may release it No ownership: Any thread may signal() No ownership: Any thread may signal()
Primary Purpose Mutual Exclusion in Critical Section Thread Synchronization / Signaling Multi-Permit Resource Pool Access
Implementation threading.Lock threading.Semaphore(1) threading.Semaphore(N)
Deadlock Prevention Guaranteed via try...finally release Careful signal sequencing required Permit count bounds concurrency

2.5 Identification of Shared State and Critical Section in the Chosen Product

In our Event Registration system, the critical section encapsulates three tightly coupled operations:

  1. Reading current remaining capacity $C_rem$.
  2. Evaluating reservation validity: if C_rem > 0.
  3. Mutating capacity ($C_rem \leftarrow C_rem - 1$) and appending the confirmed squad record to the ticket ledger.

If these operations are not executed atomically inside a Mutex barrier, interleaving causes stale reads and overbooking.

2.6 Step-by-Step Concurrency Trace (Unsafe Interleaving vs. Synchronized Execution)

The following hardware execution trace captures the microsecond contention window between two concurrent client devices (Teacher Laptop vs. Student Mobile) competing for the final available seat ($C = 1$):

Critical Section Execution & High-Contention Race Trace
Capacity: 1 Tatkal Seat Threads: 2 (Delta t = 12ms)
--- SCENARIO 1: UNSYNCHRONIZED RUN (Mutex OFF • TOCTOU Race Hazard) --- [t = 00.00ms] Thread T1 (Teacher Laptop): Evaluates if (capacity > 0) ⇒ VALID (1 > 0). Begins payment delay. [t = 12.45ms] Thread T2 (Student Mobile): Evaluates if (capacity > 0) ⇒ STALE READ! (1 > 0) VALID. Begins payment delay. [t = 30.12ms] Thread T1: Payment completed. Decrements capacity: 1 − 1 = 0. Mints TKT-01. [t = 32.88ms] Thread T2: Payment completed. Decrements capacity: 0 − 1 = −1. Mints TKT-02. ✗ ANOMALY DETECTED: Capacity = −1 < 0. Two tickets issued for 1 physical seat (OVERSOLD!). --- SCENARIO 2: MUTEX-PROTECTED RUN (threading.Lock • Dijkstra Critical Section) --- [t = 00.00ms] Thread T1 (Teacher Laptop): Requests lock: mutex.acquire() ⇒ GRANTED! Lock owner: T1. [t = 12.45ms] Thread T2 (Student Mobile): Requests lock: mutex.acquire() ⇒ BUSY! Enqueued in FIFO Queue. [t = 30.12ms] Thread T1: Completes payment. Atomically decrements capacity: 1 − 1 = 0. Confirmed TKT-01. [t = 30.25ms] Thread T1: Calls mutex.release() in finally block ⇒ Dequeues T2 and grants lock. [t = 30.35ms] Thread T2: Enters Critical Section with fresh state. Evaluates (0 > 0) ⇒ REJECTED (HTTP 409 Sold Out). [t = 30.40ms] Thread T2: System initiates automated refund & issues refund receipt: REFUND_RZP_849204. [t = 30.45ms] Thread T2: Calls mutex.release() ⇒ Final capacity = 0. ✓ SYSTEM INVARIANT PRESERVED: Remaining Capacity = 0. Exactly 1 ticket confirmed. Zero Overbooking!

Trace Analysis: Under Mutex ON, Device B's request is serialized behind Device A. When Device A releases the lock, Device B observes a fresh capacity read of $C = 0$ and is cleanly rejected with an automated refund receipt, preserving $C \ge 0$ unconditionally.

3.2 Thread Creation, Execution Lifecycle (start(), join()), and Program Structure

The multithreaded test rig utilizes the standard POSIX thread lifecycle:

  • Instantiation: Worker threads are created via threading.Thread(target=target_method, args=(squad, leader), name=thread_name).
  • start(): Invoking t.start() transitions the thread from New to Runnable, scheduling execution on the operating system kernel.
  • join(): The main thread invokes t.join() across all active threads, blocking until every concurrent transaction terminates to collect final telemetry.

3.3 Representation of Shared Data Structures and Resource Pools

The shared resource pool is modeled inside EventRegistrationSystem:

  • self.remaining_capacity: Shared integer tracking active seats ($0 \le C \le C_total$).
  • self.confirmed_tickets: Array holding confirmed TicketRecord objects.
  • self.refunded_transactions: Audit ledger storing refunded buyer records upon quota exhaustion.
  • self.audit_log: Microsecond telemetry stream recording thread states, lock acquisition, and capacity transitions.

3.4 Implementation of Unsynchronized (Unsafe) Baseline Version

The unsynchronized method (book_ticket_unsynchronized) reads capacity without lock isolation, inserts an artificial delay (simulating payment I/O), and decrements. Under 10 parallel threads competing for 2 seats, all threads read $C > 0$ during the delay window, resulting in 10 confirmed tickets and negative inventory ($C = -8$).

3.5 Implementation of Mutex (threading.Lock) / Semaphore (threading.Semaphore)

The synchronized implementation encloses critical section logic in a guaranteed barrier:

  • Mutex Architecture: Calls self.mutex.acquire(timeout=2.0). If acquired, evaluates self.remaining_capacity > 0. If valid, decrements and mints the ticket. In all execution paths, lock release is guaranteed via finally: self.mutex.release().
  • Counting Semaphore Architecture: Initializes self.counting_semaphore = threading.Semaphore(total_capacity). Each buyer thread invokes acquire() to consume one permit. Once permits drop to zero, subsequent threads are non-blockingly rejected, ensuring capacity never exceeds the permit ceiling.

3.6 Resource Release, Cancellation, Slot Reopening, and Waiting-Queue Handling

When an attendee cancels a confirmed pass, cancel_ticket(ticket_id) executes inside a mutex barrier:

  1. Locates the confirmed pass and marks its status as CANCELLED.
  2. Increments remaining_capacity += 1.
  3. Calls self.counting_semaphore.release(), signaling the reopening of a permit for waiting threads.
Deadlock & Orphan Prevention: Enclosing critical section operations inside a strict try ... finally block guarantees that release() is invoked even if an unhandled runtime error or payment timeout occurs.

4.5 Thread-Safe Integration Between Worker Threads and Dashboard Interface

The dashboard communicates with the backend concurrency kernel through asynchronous REST API calls. State mutation endpoints wrap inventory operations in the Mutex barrier. When the backend detects contention:

  • Winner Request: The backend confirms reservation, commits state to persistent storage, and returns HTTP 200 with ticket metadata. The dashboard immediately displays the VIP Boarding Pass.
  • Out-Raced Request: When capacity hits 0, the backend returns HTTP 409 (Sold Out). The client-side Fetch interceptor catches the 409 and immediately renders the Automated Refund Reassurance Modal instead of a generic error.

4.6 Complete End-to-End Request Processing Flow

The complete sequence from user click to ticket issuance or refund follows the flow illustrated in Figure 1.1:

  1. User clicks "Claim Pass" → Renders registration form.
  2. Form submission launches Razorpay checkout modal → User authorizes payment.
  3. Frontend sends transaction payload to /api/book.
  4. Backend identifies target event and queries KeyedMutexRegistry.get(eventId).
  5. Request executes inside mutex.acquire() barrier.
  6. If $C > 0$, capacity decrements, ticket records persist, and lock releases.
  7. If $C \le 0$, HTTP 409 is returned, triggering client refund modal.

CHAPTER 5 – TESTING, VALIDATION, AND OBSERVATIONS

5.1 Testing Methodology (Sequential, Concurrent Unsafe, Synchronized, Overload)

Testing followed a rigorous four-phase verification framework:

  1. Sequential Testing: Single-thread baseline verification to confirm normal inventory decrements ($5 o 4 o 3$).
  2. Concurrent Unsafe Testing: Multi-thread burst with Mutex OFF to reproduce TOCTOU race condition ($C = -1$).
  3. Concurrent Synchronized Testing: Multi-thread burst with Mutex ON to verify mutual exclusion and zero overbooking.
  4. Overload & Stress Testing: 50 concurrent synthetic threads competing for 2 seats to benchmark lock latency and fairness.

CHAPTER 6 – ERRORS, CHALLENGES, AND LEARNING OUTCOMES

6.1 Synchronization Errors Encountered (Improper Lock Scope, Deadlocks, Race Leaks)

  • E1 – Improper Lock Scope: Initially, the lock was acquired only during the capacity decrement operation, leaving the capacity check outside the protected block. This created a race leak where two threads validated $C = 1$ simultaneously before acquiring the lock.
  • E2 – Orphaned Lock / Deadlock on Exception: If payment verification or input parsing threw an unhandled exception inside the critical section, the thread crashed without invoking release(), freezing all subsequent requests perpetually.
  • E3 – Corrupt JSON Persistence under Parallel Writes: Multiple threads writing simultaneously to database.json caused file truncation and SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input.

6.2 Challenges in Thread-to-Dashboard State Refreshing

In asynchronous web applications, updating client dashboard state across concurrent worker threads presents two major challenges:

  • Stale DOM Cache: Fast-path inventory updates on the server were not immediately reflected in client browser tabs without aggressive polling or server-sent events.
  • Contention Notification Collisions: When 50 threads completed simultaneously, client-side toast notifications stacked uncontrollably, creating an overwhelming UI experience.

6.3 Root Causes and Solutions Implemented

Error / Challenge Underlying Root Cause Engineered Solution
Race Leak Read and Write operations uncoupled Expanded lock scope to enclose both validation and mutation atomically.
Deadlock / Orphan Exception bypassed release call Enclosed critical section in mandatory try ... finally { release(); } block.
File Truncation Non-atomic concurrent file I/O Implemented ACID tempfile write + atomic rename (os.replace() / fs.renameSync()).
Notification Clutter Excessive asynchronous toast emissions Replaced toast clutter with an executive Automated Refund Reassurance Modal.

6.4 Technical and Operating System Learning Outcomes

  • Dijkstra’s Invariants in Practice: Gained deep practical mastery over Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting beyond abstract textbook theory.
  • Asynchrony vs. Parallelism: Understood that single-threaded event loops (Node.js) are just as vulnerable to race conditions across I/O boundaries as multi-threaded runtimes (Python threading).
  • FIFO Starvation Immunity: Confirmed empirically that array-backed FIFO wait queues eliminate thread starvation ($O(k)$ bounded wait).

  • Procedural SVG QR Boarding Pass: Pure client-side zero-dependency QR code generator ($21 imes 21$ matrix) embedding attendee metadata and verification hash for venue check-in.
  • Live 2-Device Contention Rig (/admin): Real-time demonstration station allowing side-by-side contention testing between a teacher’s laptop and student’s mobile device with live Mutex ON/OFF toggles.
  • Keyed Lock Registry: Independent lock allocation per event resource, preventing Amdahl serialization bottlenecks across unrelated events.

93# Atomic Check within isolated Critical Section
94if self.remaining_capacity > 0:

96time.sleep(0.005)
97self.remaining_capacity -= 1

100self.confirmed_tickets.append(record)
101 
102self._log_audit("MUTEX_CONFIRM", squad_name, thread_name, "SUCCESS",

153def cancel_ticket(self, ticket_id: str, squad_name: str) -> bool:
154with self.mutex:
155target = next((t for t in self.confirmed_tickets if t.ticket_id == ticket_id and t.status == "CONFIRMED"), None)
156if target:
157target.status = "CANCELLED"
158self.remaining_capacity += 1
159self.counting_semaphore.release() # Signal() permit reopening
160self._log_audit("SLOT_REOPENED", squad_name, threading.current_thread().name,
161"CANCELLED", f"Ticket {ticket_id} cancelled. Slot reopened. New capacity: {self.remaining_capacity}")
162return True
163return False

APPENDIX B – FUNCTION-WISE / BLOCK-WISE EXPLANATION OF CODE

1. `EventRegistrationSystem.__init__()` State Initialization

  • self.remaining_capacity = total_capacity: Shared state tracking remaining seats ($C$).
  • self.mutex = threading.Lock(): Binary mutex primitive providing mutual exclusion.
  • self.counting_semaphore = threading.Semaphore(total_capacity): Counting semaphore initialized with total ticket permits.
  • self.audit_log = []: Thread-safe in-memory audit ledger recording all microsecond state transitions.

2. `book_ticket_unsynchronized()` (TOCTOU Race Hazard)

  • Time-of-Check: Reads current_slots = self.remaining_capacity without acquiring a lock.
  • Preemption Gap: Executes time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.03)) simulating network/payment I/O. Other concurrent threads enter and read the same stale value.
  • Time-of-Use: Writes self.remaining_capacity = current_slots - 1, resulting in negative capacity and overbooking.

3. `book_ticket_mutex()` (Dijkstra Critical Section Protection)

  • Entry Barrier: Calls self.mutex.acquire(timeout=2.0). Arriving threads are suspended in an OS FIFO wait queue if the lock is held.
  • Critical Section: Once inside, evaluates self.remaining_capacity > 0. If valid, decrements and mints ticket; if exhausted, logs refund tracking.
  • Exit Barrier: finally: self.mutex.release() guarantees lock handoff to the next waiting thread, eliminating deadlocks.

4. `book_ticket_semaphore()` (Permit-Based Access)

  • Calls self.counting_semaphore.acquire(blocking=True, timeout=1.0). Decrements permit counter. Once permits drop to 0, subsequent threads are immediately rejected.

5. `cancel_ticket()` (Slot Reopening & Permit Signaling)

  • Marks ticket as cancelled, increments remaining_capacity += 1, and calls self.counting_semaphore.release() to signal permit availability.
